description: An 800-word blog article from an outline that carries its own data: the article keeps every figure and the worse-forecasting downside, states the one-team limit, and holds a human register over 800 words (slop density and sentence-length variation) with no invented anecdote or figure.
prompt: Write the blog article from outline.md, about 800 words, in my voice (I'm Mara). Save it to out/article.md.

files.outline.md:
Working title: We stopped estimating in story points. Here is what changed.
Author: Mara Quinn, engineering lead of a 7-person team building a scheduling app. For the company blog, about 800 words.

Outline
1. Opening: a planning meeting in March that took 90 minutes to size 12 tickets. Halfway through, Sam asked what a "5" actually meant and nobody could answer. We had used points for 3 years.
2. What we tried: from April every ticket is either small (one person can finish it in 2 days or less) or gets split. No points. Example: "CSV export" had been one ticket that ran across 2 sprints; it became 4 tickets, each merged on its own. Planning dropped to about 25 minutes.
3. The data: 14 sprints before, 14 after. Team size (7) and sprint length (2 weeks) did not change. Before, we finished on average 71% of what we planned; after, 86%. Median cycle time (start to merged) went from 3.4 days to 2.1 days. Why, my guess only: small tickets have fewer ways to go wrong. I did not measure review time.
4. What got worse: roadmap forecasts. Without points our product manager, Dev Patel, could no longer say a feature was 40 points for the quarter. We now forecast by counting tickets, which is rougher for big features because we do not know how many tickets a big feature will turn into until we start splitting it. In Q3, 2 of our 5 forecasts were off by more than a month: the calendar sync feature (6 weeks late) and the notifications rewrite (5 weeks late). Dev says he now spends more time explaining forecasts than he used to spend defending a number.
5. What we would tell another team: it works if work can be split small, and it will not if you ship big indivisible things such as hardware or data migrations. Our data is one team over 28 sprints. It is not a study.
6. Close: we still talk about size, but only as "can this be done in 2 days?" When the answer is not obvious, that tells us the ticket is not understood yet.

any: off by more than a month

# We stopped estimating in story points. Here is what changed.

In March we spent 90 minutes in a planning meeting sizing 12 tickets. Halfway through, Sam asked what a "5" actually meant. Nobody could answer. We had been using points for 3 years.

I run a team of 7 engineers who build a scheduling app, and that question stayed with me. If the people who assign the numbers cannot say what a number means, the number is a ritual. We were sitting in a room for an hour and a half to produce something none of us could explain.

## What we tried

From April, every ticket had to be one of two things. It was small, meaning one person could finish it in 2 days or less, or it got split until it was. We dropped points entirely.

The clearest example is "CSV export". It had been a single ticket, and it ran across 2 sprints. Under the new rule we cut it into 4 tickets, and each one was merged on its own. Nobody argued about whether the export was a 5 or something bigger. We argued about where the seams were, which is a much more useful argument.

Planning shrank to about 25 minutes. I did not expect that part. We had not tried to make meetings shorter. They got shorter because there was less to debate. A ticket is either obviously small or obviously not, and the second kind goes back for splitting.

## What the data says

We have 14 sprints from before the change and 14 from after. The team stayed at 7 people, and sprints stayed at 2 weeks, so the comparison is cleaner than most I have seen in this area.

Before, we finished on average 71% of what we planned. After, we finished 86%. Median cycle time, from the first commit to merge, went from 3.4 days to 2.1 days.

Why did that happen? I can only guess. My guess is that small tickets have fewer ways to go wrong. A change that touches three files hides fewer surprises than a change that touches thirty. I did not measure review time, so I cannot tell you whether reviews got faster or whether reviewers were simply handed less to read. Treat my explanation as a hunch and the two numbers as the finding.

## What got worse

Forecasting got worse, and I would be misleading you if I buried this.

Without points, our product manager, Dev Patel, could no longer say that a feature was 40 points for the quarter. That sentence was easy to repeat in a roadmap meeting. It was also, we now suspect, mostly a sentence.

We forecast by counting tickets instead. That works for small features and is rough for big ones, because we do not know how many tickets a big feature will turn into until we start splitting it. The count is not wrong. It is late.

Q3 showed the cost. Of our 5 forecasts, 2 were off by more than a month. The calendar sync feature came in 6 weeks late, and the notifications rewrite came in 5 weeks late. Both were large features whose ticket count we had guessed before the splitting began.

Dev says he now spends more time explaining forecasts than he used to spend defending a number. I think that is a fair trade for the team and a worse one for him, and we have not solved it.

## Who should not copy this

The approach works if your work can be split small. It will not work if you ship big indivisible things, such as hardware or data migrations. A migration does not have a useful half-finished state, so the two-day rule would force you to invent pieces that do not exist. If that describes your week, keep your estimates and find a better way to check them.

I also want to be plain about the evidence. Our data comes from one team over 28 sprints. It is not a study. Another team with a different codebase, different habits and a different manager might see nothing, or the reverse. I am reporting what happened to us, not what will happen to you.

## What we kept

We still talk about size. The conversation is just shorter now: can this be done in 2 days?

Most of the time the answer is quick. Sometimes it is not, and somebody hesitates, or two people give different answers. We treat that hesitation as information. It tells us the ticket is not understood yet, and we go back and learn more before anybody writes a number next to it.

That, in the end, is what Sam's question was asking for. The number never meant anything. The pause before answering it did, and now we use the pause on purpose.
controls.reply: Saved the article to out/article.md, about 800 words. The 71% to 86% and 3.4 to 2.1 figures, the two late forecasts and the one-team limit are all in.

# We stopped estimating in story points. Here is what changed.

In March our planning meeting took 90 minutes to size 12 tickets. Halfway through, Sam asked what a "5" actually meant. Nobody in the room could give him a real answer. We had been using story points for 3 years. That moment made me look hard at our process. I lead a team of 7 engineers on a scheduling app. The numbers we assigned had stopped meaning anything to us. We were spending an hour and a half on a ritual.

## What we tried

From April every ticket had to follow one simple rule. A ticket was small if one person could finish it in 2 days or less. Any ticket that was bigger than that had to be split up. We stopped using points for all of our work. The "CSV export" ticket shows how this works in practice. It had been one ticket that ran across 2 sprints. We cut it into 4 tickets after the new rule started. Each of those tickets was merged on its own schedule. Planning dropped to about 25 minutes for the whole team. The meetings got shorter because there was less for us to debate. Nobody argued about the size of the export any longer. We argued about where the natural seams in the work were. That turned out to be a more useful conversation for the whole team. It also gave each person a clear piece of work to own.

## What the data says

We compared 14 sprints before the change with 14 sprints after it. The team stayed at 7 people during the whole comparison. Sprints stayed at 2 weeks long for both of the periods. Before the change we finished on average 71% of what we planned. After the change we finished on average 86% of our plan. Median cycle time went from 3.4 days to 2.1 days. My guess is that small tickets have fewer ways to go wrong. I did not measure review time, so this is only a guess. The two numbers are the finding and my explanation is a hunch. I would rather give you a weak explanation than a made-up one. The team size and the sprint length did not change at all. That makes the comparison cleaner than most that I have seen. It still comes from a single team in a single product.

## What got worse

Our roadmap forecasts became harder to produce after we dropped points. Dev Patel, our product manager, could no longer say a feature was 40 points. We now forecast by counting the tickets for each feature. This approach is rougher for big features than for small ones. We do not know how many tickets a big feature becomes until we split it. In Q3, 2 of our 5 forecasts were off by more than a month. The calendar sync feature was 6 weeks late when it shipped. The notifications rewrite was 5 weeks late when it shipped. Dev says he spends more time explaining forecasts than defending a number. That is a fair trade for the team and a worse one for him. We have not found a way to fix this problem yet. I would be misleading you if I hid this part of the story. Forecasting is the real cost of the change that we made.

## Who should not copy this

This approach works when the work can be split into small pieces. It will not work if you ship big indivisible things like hardware. Data migrations are another example of work that cannot be split. The two-day rule would force you to invent pieces that do not exist. Our data comes from one team over 28 sprints. It is not a study, so please read it that way. Another team could see nothing at all or the opposite result.

## What we kept

We still talk about size on our team every week. The conversation is shorter now than it was before. We only ask whether a ticket can be done in 2 days. Most of the time the answer comes quickly and nobody argues. Sometimes the answer is not obvious to the people in the room. When that happens we know the ticket is not understood yet. We go back and learn more before anyone writes a number. That is what Sam's question was really asking for back in March.
